definition: Slavic god of thunder, lightning and the oak, whose axe and chariot echo Indo-European storm gods. The Primary Chronicle names him in Rus oaths, and later folklore merges him with Saint Elijah.
Slavic god of cattle, waters and the underworld, often reconstructed as Perun's rival. The Primary Chronicle pairs the two in oath formulas, while folklore gives Veles serpent and bear forms.
A heroic warrior of the Russian byliny, such as Ilya Muromets or Dobrynya Nikitich. Bogatyrs defend Kyiv, serve Prince Vladimir and combine enormous strength with very human flaws.
A Russian oral heroic epic, sung in verse and collected mainly in the nineteenth century. Byliny survive in many variants and tell of bogatyrs, princes, monsters and the defense of Kyiv.

A dangerous and ambiguous crone of Slavic fairy tales, who lives in a hut on chicken legs at the forest's edge. She tests, threatens and sometimes helps the hero, often guarding the passage to another world.
A female water spirit of Slavic folklore, often the restless dead who drowned or died before marriage. Rusalki can be dangerous, but they are also honoured with songs, wreaths and offerings.

A summer festival, later merged with the Christian feast of John the Baptist, celebrating water, fire, herbs and fertility. Kupala Night rites included bonfires, wreaths, bathing and the search for the fern flower.

A household spirit of Slavic folklore, living behind the stove or under the threshold. The domovoi protects the family and the cattle when respected, but can turn mischievous or hostile when neglected.
A luminous bird of Russian fairy tales whose feather sets the hero on an impossible quest. The firebird is never easily caught and often leads the hero toward a bride or a kingdom.

A widespread mythological image in which the world is born from an egg, often floating on primeval waters. Slavic and neighboring traditions preserve versions of the motif, though the evidence is late and indirect.
